topicTitle: Scope Chains, Hoisting & The Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ)

lessons.title: Scope Levels: Global, Function, and Block Scope
lessons.description: Variables exist in specific scopes — understanding scope determines where your variables can be accessed.

sections.heading: What is scope?
paragraphs: Scope determines where a variable can be accessed in your code. Think of it as boundaries — a variable lives in its scope and can be reached from nested scopes, but not from outside.
list: Global scope — variables declared outside any function or block; accessible everywhere
Function scope — variables declared inside a function; only accessible within that function
Block scope — variables declared with let/const inside {}; only accessible within that block
var creates function scope, not block scope — a common source of bugs

codeExamples.heading: Scope in action
explanation: let and const are block-scoped — they only exist inside the nearest {}.
var is function-scoped — it leaks out of blocks into the function.
Global variables are accessible from any scope.
Inner scopes can access outer scopes, but not the reverse.

practice.task: Create variables at global, function, and block scope levels. Try accessing each from different locations and document which accesses succeed and which fail.
hints: Declare a global variable outside any function.
Declare a function-scoped variable with let inside a function.
Declare a block-scoped variable inside an if statement.
Try accessing each from the others.

keyTakeaways: Global scope variables are accessible everywhere in your code.
Function scope (var) means the variable is available throughout the function.
Block scope (let/const) means the variable is only available within the nearest {}.
Inner scopes can see outer scope variables, but outer scopes cannot see inner ones.
lessons.challenge: Predict the output of a code snippet with nested scopes before running it, then verify in the console.

lessons.title: Lexical Scope Lookup Chains
lessons.description: When a variable isn't found in the current scope, JavaScript looks up the chain to outer scopes.

sections.heading: How scope lookup works
paragraphs: When JavaScript encounters a variable, it searches from the current scope outward. If the variable isn't found in any scope up to the global scope, it throws a ReferenceError. This chain is called the scope chain.
list: JavaScript searches inward-to-outward: current scope → parent → grandparent → global
Once found, the search stops — inner scopes can shadow outer variables
The scope chain is determined at function creation time (lexical scoping)
Each function remembers the scope where it was defined, not where it's called

codeExamples.heading: Scope chain traversal
explanation: inner can't find a or b locally, so it looks outward.
It finds b in outer's scope and a in global scope.
The scope chain is: inner → outer → global.
JavaScript resolves variables by walking up this chain until it finds a match.

practice.task: Create 3 nested scopes with a variable in each. Log a variable from the outermost scope inside the innermost function to see the full scope chain traversal.
hints: Create global, function, and inner function with variables at each level.
From the innermost function, log the global variable.
JavaScript walks up: inner → outer → global to find it.

keyTakeaways: Scope lookup goes from inner to outer until the variable is found or a ReferenceError is thrown.
Lexical scoping means a function's scope is determined by where it's written, not where it's called.
Inner variables can shadow (hide) outer variables with the same name.
The scope chain is fixed at function creation time and never changes.
lessons.challenge: Write code where an inner function shadows a global variable name. Verify which value the inner function sees.

lessons.title: Function & Variable Hoisting Mechanics (var vs let/const)
lessons.description: Hoisting moves declarations to the top — but let/const and function expressions behave differently.

sections.heading: What is hoisting?
paragraphs: Hoisting is JavaScript's behavior of moving declarations to the top of their scope during the creation phase. But not all declarations are hoisted the same way.
list: Function declarations are fully hoisted — name and body are available immediately
var is hoisted but initialized as undefined
let and const are hoisted but NOT initialized — they're in the TDZ
Function expressions and arrow functions follow their variable's hoisting rules

codeExamples.heading: Hoisting differences
explanation: Function declarations are available everywhere in their scope.
var variables are hoisted but start as undefined — confusing but not an error.
let/const are in the TDZ — accessing them throws a ReferenceError.
Function expressions follow their variable type — a let function expression is in TDZ.

practice.task: Write code that demonstrates all three hoisting behaviors: function declaration, var, and let. Show which ones work before their declaration line and which don't.
hints: Call a function declaration before its definition line.
Log a var before its declaration — gets undefined.
Log a let before its declaration — throws ReferenceError.

keyTakeaways: Function declarations are fully hoisted — you can call them before they appear in the code.
var is hoisted but initialized as undefined, leading to confusing behavior.
let and const are in the Temporal Dead Zone — reading them before declaration throws an error.
Always declare variables at the top of their scope to avoid hoisting surprises.
lessons.challenge: Refactor a snippet that uses var to use let instead. Explain every difference in behavior before and after the refactor.

lessons.title: The Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ) & Reference Errors
lessons.description: The TDZ is the period between a variable's creation and its declaration — accessing it throws a ReferenceError.

sections.heading: What is the TDZ?
paragraphs: When JavaScript creates a let or const variable during the creation phase, it reserves the name but doesn't initialize it. From that moment until the declaration line executes, the variable is in the Temporal Dead Zone — reading it throws a ReferenceError.
list: TDZ starts when the scope is entered (creation phase)
TDZ ends when the declaration line is executed
Only affects let, const and class declarations
var doesn't have a TDZ — it's initialized as undefined instead
The TDZ is a safety feature that prevents using uninitialized variables

codeExamples.heading: TDZ in different scenarios
explanation: The TDZ error occurs because a exists in scope but hasn't been initialized yet.
Block-scoped let/const variables have their own TDZ within their block.
typeof is safe for truly undeclared variables but still fails in the TDZ.
var avoids the TDZ entirely by initializing as undefined.

practice.task: Write a function with a let variable and try to access it before the declaration in at least 3 different scenarios (normal access, typeof, and inside an if block).
hints: Try accessing a block-scoped let inside its block before the declaration line.

keyTakeaways: The TDZ prevents accessing let/const variables before they're initialized.
This is a safety feature that catches bugs early — use it to your advantage.
var doesn't have a TDZ — it starts as undefined, which can hide bugs.
Always declare variables at the top of their scope to avoid TDZ errors.
lessons.challenge: Explain the TDZ to a beginner using a real-world analogy (e.g., a gift box that hasn't been opened yet).
